summary:
Split a rotated sorted list anywhere and **at least one side is sorted**. A sorted side has a known range
(its two ends), so you can tell instantly whether the target could be in it. Go there if so, otherwise to the
other side. One binary search, O(log n).

question.md:
Distinct ids were sorted, then rotated. Return the target's index, or −1, in O(log n).

- **Unknown rotation point.** It could even be zero (fully sorted).
- **Distinct values,** so comparisons between ends are reliable. (With repeats see **Rotated Shelf With
  Repeats**.)

think.md:
Take `[21, 25, 30, 34, 2, 7, 11, 16]` and target 7. Split at the middle (index 3, value 34).
The left half `[21, 25, 30, 34]` happens to be sorted; the right half contains the drop.

think.caption: The sorted half (shaded) covers exactly the values between its two ends.

think.md:
A sorted half covers exactly the values between its first and last element. 7 is not between
21 and 34, so it can't be in the left half: go right. Repeat on the new range: again one side
of its middle is sorted. Which side is sorted? If `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]`, the left side is (no drop inside it);
otherwise the right side is.

Alternatively, first find the rotation point (the minimum) with one binary search, then run an ordinary binary
search on whichever run could contain the target. Same complexity, two searches.

approaches.title: Linear search
build: Return the index where the value equals the target, or −1.

limits.md: Ignores that the list is two sorted runs; the requirement is O(log n).

approaches.title: Find the rotation point, then search one run

idea.md: Binary-search the minimum's index `p` (compare with the last element). The list is then `[p … n − 1]` and `[0 … p − 1]`, both sorted. If `a[p] ≤ target ≤ a[n − 1]`, binary-search the first run; otherwise the second.

build: Find `p`, the index of the minimum.
Pick the run whose value range could contain the target.
Classic binary search in that run.

lines.text: Index of the minimum, found by comparing with the last element (as in **Rotation Low Point**).
The low run `[p, n − 1]` holds values from `a[p]` to `a[n − 1]`; if the target is in that range, search there, else in the high run `[0, p − 1]`.
An ordinary binary search inside one sorted run.

notes.cpp: `lower_bound` over the chosen run, then check equality.

complexity.md: **Time O(log n):** two binary searches. **Space O(1).**

steps.text: lo=0, hi=7, mid=3: 34 > 16, so the drop (and the minimum) is right of mid: lo = 4.
lo=4, hi=7, mid=5: 7 < 16, so mid … hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or left of it: hi = 5.
lo=4, hi=5, mid=4: 2 < 7, so mid … hi is sorted and the minimum is at mid or left of it: hi = 4.
The low run starts at 4. 7 is between 2 and 16, so search indices 4…7.

walk.title: First find the rotation point (the minimum). Then the target lies in one of the two sorted runs: binary-search that run.

limits.md: Already optimal, but it needs two separate searches and an extra decision. The one-pass version folds both into a single loop.

approaches.title: One-pass search on the sorted half

idea.md: At each step: if `a[mid]` is the target, done. If `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]`, the left half is sorted: go left if `a[lo] ≤ target < a[mid]`, else right. Otherwise the right half is sorted: go right if `a[mid] < target ≤ a[hi]`, else left.

build: Decide which half is sorted with `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]`.
Check whether the target lies within that half's end values; move accordingly.

lines.text: `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]` means no drop between lo and mid: that half is sorted and holds exactly the values `a[lo] … a[mid]`. Go there only if the target is in that range.
Otherwise the drop is in the left half, so the right half `a[mid] … a[hi]` is sorted; same test on it.

steps.text: lo=0, hi=7, mid=3: left half 21…34 is sorted; 7 is not inside it: go right.

walk.title: One pass: at least one half around mid is sorted. If the target fits inside the sorted half's range, go there; otherwise go to the other half.

takeaways.md:
- In a rotated sorted array, **one half around mid is always sorted**; test whether the target lies in that
  half's value range.
- `a[lo] ≤ a[mid]` identifies a sorted left half (with distinct values).
- Equivalent two-step method: find the rotation point, then search one run.
